replacement: “This, then, is what Hellenic law entitles us to demand as a right. But we also have advice to offer and claims on your gratitude. Since there is no danger of our injuring you, as we are not enemies, and since our friendship does not amount to very frequent intercourse, we say that these claims ought to be settled at the present juncture. When you needed warships for the war against the Aeginetans, before the Persian invasion, Corinth supplied you with twenty vessels. That good turn, and the line we took on the Samian question, when we were the reason the Peloponnesians refused to assist them, enabled you to conquer Aegina and to punish Samos. And we acted thus at crises when, if ever, men are apt to forget everything for the sake of victory in their efforts against their enemies. They regard the man who assists them then as a friend, even if he has been a foe until now, and the man who opposes them then as a foe, even if he has been a friend until now. Indeed they allow their real interests to suffer from their absorbing preoccupation with the struggle.

After the rout, the Corinthians did not bother to lash fast and tow away the hulls of the vessels they had disabled. Instead they turned on the men, whom they butchered as they sailed through, caring less to take prisoners. They even killed some of their own friends by mistake, not knowing that their right wing had been defeated. For the number of ships on both sides, and the distance over which they covered the sea, made it hard, once the fleets had joined, to tell conquerors from conquered. This battle proved far greater than any before it, at least any between Hellenes, in the number of vessels engaged. After the Corinthians had chased the Corcyraeans to land, they turned to the wrecks and their dead. They succeeded in getting hold of most of these and conveying them to Sybota, the meeting place of the land forces supplied by their barbarian allies. Sybota, it must be said, is a desert harbor of Thesprotis. When this task was over, they mustered again and sailed against the Corcyraeans. The Corcyraeans advanced to meet them with all the ships they had left that were fit for service, accompanied by the Athenian vessels, for they feared that the Corinthians might attempt a landing in their territory. It was by now getting late, and the paean had been sung for the attack, when the Corinthians suddenly began to back water. They had seen twenty Athenian ships sailing up. The Athenians had sent these out afterward to reinforce the ten, fearing, as it turned out justly, that the Corcyraeans would be defeated and that their handful of ships could not protect them. The Corinthians saw these ships first. They suspected that they were from Athens and that those they saw were not all, but that more were behind. So they began to retire. The Corcyraeans had not sighted the ships, since they were advancing from a point where they could not see so well. They were wondering why the Corinthians were backing water when some caught sight of the Athenians and cried out that there were ships in view ahead. At this they also retired, for it was now getting dark, and the Corinthian retreat had suspended the fighting. So the two sides parted, and the battle ceased with night. The Corcyraeans were in their camp at Leukimme when these twenty ships from Athens, under the command of Glaucon, son of Leagrus, and Andocides, son of Leogoras, made their way through the corpses and wrecks and sailed up to the camp, not long after they had been sighted. It was now night, and the Corcyraeans feared that they might be hostile vessels. But they soon recognized them, and the ships came to anchor.

On receiving this answer from the Athenians, the Corinthians began preparing for their voyage home, and set up a trophy at Sybota, on the continent. The Corcyraeans, for their part, picked up the wrecks and dead that the current, and a wind that rose in the night, had scattered in all directions and carried out to them, and as victors they set up their own trophy at Sybota, on the island. Each side had its own reasons for claiming the victory. The Corinthians had been victorious in the sea-fight until night. This had enabled them to carry off most of the wrecks and dead, and they held no fewer than a thousand prisoners of war, and had sunk close upon seventy vessels. The Corcyraeans had destroyed about thirty ships, and after the Athenians arrived they had picked up the wrecks and dead on their own side. They had also seen the Corinthians retire before them, backing water at the sight of the Athenian vessels, and, once the Athenians had come, refuse to sail out against them from Sybota. So both sides claimed the victory.

Meanwhile the Potidæans and the Peloponnesians with Aristeus were encamped on the isthmus, on the side facing Olynthus, waiting for the Athenians, and they had set up their market outside the city. The allies had chosen Aristeus general of all the infantry, and the command of the cavalry was given to Perdiccas. He had at once left the alliance of the Athenians and gone back to that of the Potidæans, and had appointed Iolaus as his general. The plan of Aristeus was to keep his own force on the isthmus and await the Athenian attack. The Chalcidians and the allies were to stay outside the isthmus, and the two hundred cavalry of Perdiccas at Olynthus, to act on the Athenian rear when the Athenians advanced against him, so that the enemy would be placed between two fires. Meanwhile Callias the Athenian general and his colleagues sent the Macedonian horse and a few of the allies to Olynthus, to prevent any movement from that quarter. The Athenians themselves broke up their camp and marched against Potidæa. When they reached the isthmus and saw the enemy preparing for battle, they formed against him, and soon afterward the two sides engaged. The wing of Aristeus, with the Corinthians and other picked troops around him, routed the wing opposed to it and followed it a considerable distance in pursuit. But the rest of the army of the Potidæans and Peloponnesians was defeated by the Athenians and took refuge inside the fortifications. When Aristeus returned from the pursuit, he saw that the rest of the army was defeated. He was at a loss which of two risks to choose, whether to go to Olynthus or to Potidæa. In the end he decided to draw his men into as small a space as possible and force his way into Potidæa at a run. Not without difficulty, through a storm of missiles, he passed along the breakwater through the sea, and brought off most of his men safe, though a few were lost. Meanwhile the auxiliaries of the Potidæans from Olynthus, which is about seven miles off and in sight of Potidæa, had advanced a little way to help when the battle began and the signals were raised, and the Macedonian horse had formed against them to prevent it. But victory soon declared for the Athenians and the signals were taken down, and the auxiliaries retired back within the wall, while the Macedonians returned to the Athenians. So there were no cavalry present on either side. After the battle the Athenians set up a trophy and gave back their dead to the Potidæans under truce. The Potidæans and their allies had close upon three hundred killed; the Athenians had a hundred and fifty of their own citizens killed, and Callias their general.

“You are responsible for all this. It was you who first let them fortify their city after the Median war, and later build the long walls. Then and now you keep depriving of freedom not only the peoples they have enslaved but even your own allies up to now. The true author of a people’s subjugation is not so much the one who carries it out as the power that could prevent it and permits it, above all when that power claims the glory of being the liberator of Hellas. At last we are gathered here, though gathering was not easy, and even now our aims are not settled. We should no longer be asking whether we have been wronged. We should be asking how to defend ourselves. The aggressors have matured plans, and against our indecision they have put aside threats and moved to action. We know the paths along which Athenian aggression travels, and how insidiously it advances. She may take some confidence from thinking that your dullness of perception keeps you from noticing her. But that is nothing beside the impulse she will gain from knowing that you do see, and do not care to interfere. You, Lacedaemonians, alone of all the Hellenes, do nothing. You defend yourselves not by acting but by seeming about to act. You alone wait until an enemy’s power has doubled, when you could have crushed it in its infancy. Yet you had a name for being dependable; in your case, we fear, that name said more than the truth. As we ourselves know, the Mede had time to come from the ends of the earth to Peloponnese, and no force of yours worth mentioning went out to meet him. But he was a distant enemy. Athens at least is a near neighbor, and still you utterly ignore her. Against Athens you choose defense over attack, and you leave the outcome to chance by postponing the struggle until she is far stronger than she was. And you know that, on the whole, the rock on which the barbarian was wrecked was himself, and that if Athens, our present enemy, has not many times destroyed us, we owe that more to her blunders than to your protection. Indeed, hopes placed in you have before now ruined some, whose faith made them neglect to prepare.

Not long after their return from Euboea, they made a thirty years’ truce with the Lacedaemonians and their allies, and gave up the posts they held in Peloponnese — Nisaea, Pegae, Troezen, and Achaia. In the sixth year of the truce, war broke out between the Samians and Milesians over Priene. The Milesians had the worse of it and came to Athens to complain loudly against the Samians. Some private persons from Samos itself, who wanted to revolutionize the government, joined them. So the Athenians sailed to Samos with forty ships and set up a democracy. They took fifty boys and as many men from the Samians as hostages and lodged them in Lemnos; then they left a garrison in the island and returned home. But some of the Samians had not stayed in the island and had fled to the continent. They came to an agreement with the most powerful men in the city and made an alliance with Pissuthnes, son of Hystaspes, who was then satrap of Sardis. They collected a force of seven hundred mercenaries and crossed over to Samos by night. First they rose against the commons and secured most of them; next they stole their hostages from Lemnos. After that they revolted, handed over to Pissuthnes the Athenian garrison left with them, together with its commanders, and at once prepared an expedition against Miletus. The Byzantines revolted with them.

The Athenians heard the news and at once sailed against Samos with sixty ships. Sixteen of these never engaged: some went to Caria to watch for the Phoenician fleet, and others to Chios and Lesbos with orders for reinforcements. But forty-four ships under Pericles and nine colleagues gave battle off the island of Tragia to seventy Samian vessels, twenty of them transports, which were sailing from Miletus. The Athenians won. Later they were reinforced by forty ships from Athens and twenty-five Chian and Lesbian vessels. They landed, and since they were stronger on land they surrounded the city with three walls; it was also blockaded from the sea. Meanwhile word came that the Phoenician fleet was approaching to help the Samians; indeed Stesagoras and others had left the island with five ships to bring it. So Pericles took sixty ships from the blockading squadron and left in haste for Caunus and Caria. In the meantime the Samians made a sudden sally and fell on the camp, which they found unfortified. They destroyed the look-out vessels and engaged and defeated those that were launched to meet them. For fourteen days they were masters of their own seas and brought in and carried out what they pleased. But when Pericles arrived, they were shut up again. Fresh reinforcements then came — forty ships from Athens with Thucydides, Hagnon, and Phormio; twenty with Tlepolemus and Anticles; and thirty vessels from Chios and Lesbos. The Samians made a brief attempt at fighting, but could not hold out. After a siege of nine months they surrendered on conditions: they razed their walls, gave hostages, delivered up their ships, and arranged to pay the expenses of the war by installments. The Byzantines also agreed to be subject as before.

Not many years after this, we come at last to the events already related: the affairs of Corcyra and Potidæa, and the incidents that served as a pretext for the present war. All these actions of the Hellenes, against each other and against the barbarian, took place in the fifty years between the retreat of Xerxes and the beginning of this war. In that time the Athenians put their empire on a firmer footing and raised their own home power to a very great height. The Lacedaemonians saw it clearly, yet opposed it only briefly and for the most part stayed inactive. They were slow by long habit to go to war unless necessity forced them, and in this case they were also hampered by wars at home. At last the growth of Athenian power could no longer be ignored, and their own confederacy came under its encroachments. Then they felt they could endure it no longer. The time had come to throw themselves heart and soul upon the hostile power and break it, if they could, by beginning the present war. They had already made up their own minds that the treaty had been broken and that the Athenians were guilty. Even so, they sent to Delphi and asked the God whether war would be well for them. As it is reported, he answered that if they put their whole strength into the war, victory would be theirs, and he promised that he himself would be with them, whether invoked or uninvoked. Still, they wished to summon their allies again and take a vote on whether it was proper to make war. The ambassadors of the confederates arrived and a congress was convened. All spoke their minds, and most of them denounced the Athenians and demanded that the war begin. The Corinthians did so in particular. Earlier they had gone through the cities one by one on their own account, urging them to vote for war, for fear that it would come too late to save Potidæa. They were present on this occasion too, and they came forward last and spoke as follows:

The King listened to him and raised him up, with his son, as he was sitting with him in his arms in the most effective form of supplication. When the Lacedaemonians arrived not long afterwards, he refused to give Themistocles up for anything they could say. Instead he sent him off by land to the other sea, to Pydna in Alexander’s dominions, since Themistocles wished to go to the Persian king. There he met a merchant ship on the point of starting for Ionia. He went on board and was carried by a storm to the Athenian squadron that was blockading Naxos. In his alarm — luckily he was unknown to the people in the vessel — he told the master who he was and what he was fleeing from. He said that if the master refused to save him, he would declare that he was taking him for a bribe. Meanwhile their safety lay in letting no one leave the ship until a favorable time for sailing should arise. If the master complied with his wishes, he promised him a proper recompense. The master did as he asked, and after lying to for a day and a night out of reach of the squadron, at length arrived at Ephesus.

“There is one principle, Athenians, that I hold to through everything: no concession to the Peloponnesians. I know that the spirit that inspires men while they are being persuaded to make war is not always kept once they act, and that resolutions change as circumstances change. Yet I see that now, as before, the same counsel is demanded of me, almost literally the same. And I put it to those of you who are allowing yourselves to be persuaded: support the national resolves even if we meet with reverses, or else give up all credit for their wisdom if we succeed. For sometimes the course of events is as arbitrary as the plans of men; indeed this is why we usually blame chance for whatever does not happen as we expected. Now it was clear before that Lacedaemon entertained designs against us, and it is still clearer now. The treaty provides that we shall submit our differences to each other for legal settlement and that meanwhile each shall keep what it has. Yet the Lacedaemonians have never made us any such offer and have never accepted one from us. On the contrary, they wish complaints to be settled by war instead of by negotiation, and in the end we find them here dropping the tone of expostulation and adopting that of command. They order us to raise the siege of Potidæa, to let Aegina be independent, and to revoke the Megara decree, and they conclude with an ultimatum warning us to leave the Hellenes independent. I hope none of you will think that we shall be going to war for a trifle if we refuse to revoke the Megara decree. It stands in front of their complaints, and its revocation is supposed to save us from war. I hope, too, that no feeling of self-reproach will linger in your minds, as if you went to war for slight cause. Why, this trifle contains the whole seal and trial of your resolution. If you give way, you will instantly have to meet some greater demand, since you will have been frightened into obedience in the first instance, whereas a firm refusal will make them understand clearly that they must treat you more as equals. Make your decision therefore at once: either submit before you are harmed, or, if we are to go to war, as I for one think we ought, do so without caring whether the ostensible cause is great or small, resolved against making concessions and against consenting to a precarious tenure of our possessions. For every claim from an equal, urged upon a neighbor as a command before any attempt at legal settlement, whether great or small, has only one meaning, and that is slavery.

These were the charges and differences between the rival powers before the war, which arose immediately from the affair at Epidamnus and Corcyra. Even so, intercourse and mutual communication went on. It was carried on without heralds, though not without suspicion, because events were happening that amounted to a breach of the treaty and gave grounds for war.

The Plataeans then sent a messenger to Athens, returned the dead to the Thebans under a truce, and set the city in order as the emergency seemed to require. The Athenians had been told of the affair right after it happened. At once they arrested every Boeotian in Attica, and they sent a herald to the Plataeans with an order not to proceed to extremes with their Theban prisoners until Athens had given instructions. Of course the news of the men’s death had not reached them. The first messenger had left Plataea just as the Thebans entered it, and the second just after their defeat and capture, so nothing later had come. The Athenians therefore gave their orders without knowing the facts, and when the herald arrived he found the men already dead. After this the Athenians marched to Plataea, brought in provisions and left a garrison there. They also removed the women and children and the men who were of least use.

While the Peloponnesians were still assembling at the Isthmus, or were on the march before invading Attica, Pericles, son of Xanthippus, one of the ten generals of the Athenians, saw that the invasion was coming. Archidamus happened to be his friend, and Pericles conceived that Archidamus might possibly pass over his estate and leave it unravaged. Archidamus might do so out of a personal wish to oblige him, or on instructions from Lacedaemon meant to set people against him, as had already been tried in the demand for the expulsion of the accursed family. So Pericles took a precaution. He declared in the assembly that, although Archidamus was his friend, the friendship would not be allowed to damage the state. If the enemy made an exception of his houses and lands and did not pillage them like the rest, he gave them up to the public at once, so that they could not bring him under suspicion. He also gave the citizens advice on their present affairs, in the same spirit as before. They should prepare for the war and bring their property in from the country. They should not go out to battle, but come into the city and guard it, and make ready their fleet, in which their real strength lay. They should also keep a tight rein on their allies. The strength of Athens came from the money that the allies’ payments brought in, and success in war depended chiefly on conduct and capital, so there was no reason for despair. Leaving other sources of income aside, the tribute of the allies brought in an average revenue of six hundred talents of silver. There were still six thousand talents of coined silver on the Acropolis, out of nine thousand seven hundred that had once been there; the money for the porch of the Acropolis, the other public buildings and Potidæa had been taken from this sum. This did not include the uncoined gold and silver in public and private offerings, the sacred vessels used in the processions and games, the Median spoils and similar resources, which amounted to five hundred talents. To this he added the treasures of the other temples, which were by no means small and could fairly be used. Indeed, if they were ever absolutely driven to it, they could take even the gold ornaments of Athene herself. The statue held forty talents of pure gold, and all of it could be removed. They could use this for their survival, but every penny of it must be restored. Such was their financial position, and surely it was a satisfactory one. Next, they had an army of thirteen thousand heavy infantry, besides sixteen thousand more in the garrisons and on duty at home in Athens. This was the number on guard at first, in the event of an invasion; it was made up of the oldest and youngest levies and of those resident aliens who had heavy armor. The Phaleric wall ran four miles before it joined the wall around the city. Of the wall around the city nearly five miles were guarded, though part of it was left without a guard, namely the part between the Long Wall and the Phaleric. Then there were the Long Walls to Piraeus, a distance of some four miles and a half, and the outer one was manned. Finally, the circumference of Piraeus together with Munychia was nearly seven miles and a half, but only half of it was guarded. Pericles also showed them that they had twelve hundred horse, counting mounted archers, sixteen hundred archers on foot, and three hundred galleys fit for service. These were the resources of Athens in each department when the Peloponnesian invasion was impending and hostilities were beginning. Pericles also urged his usual arguments for expecting a favorable outcome of the war.

“Our constitution does not copy the laws of our neighbors. We are a pattern to others rather than imitators of them. Our administration favors the many instead of the few, and that is why it is called a democracy. In private disputes the laws give equal justice to all. As for social standing, advancement in public life goes to reputation for capacity, and class considerations are not allowed to interfere with merit. Nor does poverty bar the way: a man who can serve the state is not hindered by the obscurity of his condition. The freedom we enjoy in public life extends also to our ordinary life. In that, far from keeping a jealous watch on one another, we do not feel called upon to be angry with a neighbor for doing as he likes, or even to give him those injurious looks which cannot fail to give offense, though they inflict no actual penalty. But this ease in our private relations does not make us lawless as citizens. Fear is our chief safeguard against that. It teaches us to obey the magistrates and the laws, above all those that protect the injured, whether they are actually on the statute book or belong to the unwritten code that cannot be broken without acknowledged disgrace.

“We also provide plenty of ways for the mind to refresh itself after business. We celebrate games and sacrifices all the year round, and the elegance of our private establishments gives daily pleasure and helps to banish gloom. And because our city is so large, the produce of the whole world is drawn into our harbor, so that the Athenian enjoys the fruits of other countries as familiarly as those of his own.

“These are not the only points in which our city deserves admiration. We cultivate refinement without extravagance and knowledge without softness. We employ wealth more for use than for show, and we think the real disgrace of poverty lies not in admitting to it but in not struggling against it. Our public men also have private affairs to attend to, and our ordinary citizens, though busy with their trades, are still fair judges of public matters. We are unlike any other nation in this: we regard a man who takes no part in these duties as useless, not as unambitious. We Athenians can at all events judge a proposal, even if we cannot originate one; and we do not see discussion as a stumbling-block in the way of action. We think it an indispensable preliminary to any wise action at all. In our enterprises, again, we present the singular spectacle of daring and deliberation, each carried to its highest point and both united in the same persons, although decision is usually the fruit of ignorance, and hesitation of reflection. But the palm of courage will surely be awarded most justly to those who know best the difference between hardship and pleasure and yet are never tempted to shrink from danger. In generosity, too, we are singular, since we win our friends by conferring favors, not by receiving them. Yet of course the giver of a favor is the firmer friend of the two, wishing by continued kindness to keep the recipient in his debt. The debtor feels less keenly, because he knows that his return will be a payment, not a free gift. And only the Athenians, fearless of consequences, confer their benefits not out of calculations of expediency but in the confidence of liberality.

“If I have dwelt at some length on the character of our country, it was to show that we have more at stake in this struggle than men who have no such blessings to lose, and at the same time to establish by definite proofs the panegyric of the men over whom I am now speaking. That panegyric is now largely complete. The Athens I have celebrated is only what the heroism of these men and their like has made her; and their fame, unlike that of most Hellenes, will be found to match their deserts exactly. If a test of worth is wanted, it lies in the way they ended their lives. This holds not only where that ending set the final seal on a man’s merit, but also where it gave the first sign that he had any. For it is just to claim that steadfastness in his country’s battles should cover a man’s other imperfections like a cloak: the good action has blotted out the bad, and his merit as a citizen has more than outweighed his faults as an individual. Yet none of these men let wealth, with its prospect of future enjoyment, unnerve his spirit, or let poverty, with its hope of a day of freedom and riches, tempt him to shrink from danger. No: they held vengeance upon their enemies to be more desirable than any personal blessing, and reckoned it the most glorious of hazards. So they joyfully chose to accept the risk, to make sure of their vengeance, and to let their wishes wait. They committed to hope the uncertainty of final success, but in the business before them they thought it right to act boldly and trust in themselves. Choosing to die resisting rather than to live submitting, they fled only from dishonor, but met danger face to face; and after one brief moment, at the summit of their fortune, they escaped, not from their fear, but from their glory.

“So died these men, as became Athenians. You, their survivors, must resolve to have as unfaltering a spirit in the field, though you may pray for a happier outcome. Do not be content with ideas drawn only from words about the advantages of defending your country. A speaker could make a valuable text of these even before an audience as alive to them as this one. You must yourselves realize the power of Athens and feed your eyes upon her from day to day, until love of her fills your hearts. Then, when all her greatness has broken upon you, reflect that men won it by courage, a sense of duty, and a keen feeling of honor in action. Reflect too that when they failed in some enterprise, they would not consent to deprive their country of their valor, but laid it at her feet as the most glorious contribution they could offer. All of them gave their lives in common, and each of them received individually that renown which never grows old. They received also a sepulchre: not so much the one where their bones lie, as that noblest of shrines in which their glory is stored up, to be remembered forever whenever deed or story calls for its commemoration. For heroes have the whole earth for their tomb. In lands far from their own, where the column with its epitaph declares it, there is enshrined in every breast an unwritten record, with no tablet to preserve it except that of the heart. Take these men as your model. Judge happiness to be the fruit of freedom, and freedom of valor, and never decline the dangers of war. For it is not the wretched, who have nothing to hope for, who would most justly be unsparing of their lives. It is rather those to whom continued life may bring reverses as yet unknown, and for whom a fall, if it came, would have the most tremendous consequences. And surely, to a man of spirit, the degradation of cowardice is immeasurably more grievous than the unfelt death that strikes him in the midst of his strength and patriotism!

“Comfort, therefore, not condolence, is what I have to offer to those parents of the dead who are here. They know that life is subject to numberless chances; but fortunate are those who draw as their lot a death as glorious as the one that has caused your mourning, and whose lives have been measured so exactly that they end in the happiness in which they were spent. Still, I know this is a hard saying, especially since you will constantly be reminded of the dead when you see in other people’s homes the blessings in which you once took pride. For grief is felt not so much for the want of what we have never known as for the loss of what we have long been used to. Yet you who are still of an age to have children must bear up in the hope of having others in their place. They will help you to forget those you have lost, and they will be to the state both a reinforcement and a security; for no fair or just policy can be expected from a citizen who does not, like his fellows, bring a father’s interests and apprehensions to the decision. As for those of you who are past your prime, you must count it a gain that the best part of your life was fortunate, and that the short span that remains will be cheered by the fame of the departed. For only the love of honor never grows old; and what rejoices the heart of age and helplessness is honor, not gain, as some would have it.

“To the sons or brothers of the dead I turn next, and I see a hard struggle before you. When a man is gone, everyone is accustomed to praise him. However transcendent your merit, you will find it difficult not only to overtake their renown but even to come near it. The living have envy to contend with, while those who are no longer in our path are honored with a goodwill that rivalry does not touch. And if I must say something on the subject of female excellence to those of you who will now be widows, one short exhortation will contain it all. Great will be your glory if you do not fall short of your natural character, and greatest will be the glory of the woman who is least talked of among the men, whether for good or for bad.

“My task is now finished. I have performed it as well as I could, and as far as words go, the requirements of the law are satisfied. As for deeds, those who lie buried here have already received part of their honors, and the rest they will receive through their children, who will be brought up at public expense until they are grown. In this way the state offers a valuable prize, like the garland of victory in this race of valor, both to those who have fallen and to their survivors. And where the rewards for merit are greatest, there the best citizens are found.

That year, by general admission, was otherwise unprecedentedly free from sickness, and the few ordinary cases that did occur all ended in this disease. As a rule, however, there was no visible cause. People in good health were suddenly seized by violent heats in the head, with redness and inflammation of the eyes. The inward parts, such as the throat and tongue, turned bloody and gave off an unnatural, foul breath. Sneezing and hoarseness followed, and soon the pain reached the chest and brought on a hard cough. When it settled in the stomach, it upset it, and there came discharges of bile of every kind that physicians have named, with very great distress. In most cases an ineffectual retching followed, causing violent spasms; in some these ended soon afterward, in others much later. Outwardly the body was not very hot to the touch, nor pale, but reddish and livid, breaking out in small pustules and ulcers. Inwardly, though, it burned so fiercely that the patients could not bear to have even the lightest clothing or linen on them, and would rather be stark naked. What they wanted most was to throw themselves into cold water. Some of the neglected sick did so, plunging into the rain-tanks in their agony of unquenchable thirst; but it made no difference whether they drank little or much. On top of this, the wretched feeling of being unable to rest or sleep tormented them without ceasing. While the disease was at its height the body did not waste away, but withstood its ravages remarkably well. So when most patients died, on the seventh or eighth day, of the inward burning, they still had some strength left. But if they got past that stage and the disease descended further into the bowels, causing violent ulceration there with severe diarrhea, the resulting weakness was generally fatal. The disorder began in the head, ran its course from there through the whole body, and even where it did not kill, it left its mark on the extremities. It settled in the privy parts, the fingers and the toes, and many escaped with the loss of these, some also with the loss of their eyes. Others, on first recovering, were seized by a total loss of memory and knew neither themselves nor their friends.

Such, then, setting aside the many peculiar variations from case to case, were the general features of the distemper. Meanwhile the city was free of all the usual disorders, or if any case occurred, it ended in this. Some died neglected, others in the midst of every attention. No remedy was found that could be used as a specific, for what helped in one case harmed in another. Strong and weak constitutions proved equally unable to resist; all alike were swept away, even those who were dieted with the utmost care. By far the most terrible feature of the malady was the dejection that came over anyone who felt himself sickening. The despair into which they instantly fell took away their power of resistance and made them a much easier prey to the disease. Besides this, there was the awful sight of men dying like sheep after catching the infection from nursing one another. This caused the greatest mortality. If they were afraid to visit one another, they perished from neglect; indeed many houses were emptied of their inmates for lack of a nurse. If, on the other hand, they ventured to visit, death was the result. This was especially so with those who made any claim to goodness. Honor made them spare themselves nothing in attending their friends in their houses, where even the members of the family were at last worn out by the moans of the dying and gave way to the force of the disaster. Yet it was those who had recovered from the disease who showed most compassion to the sick and the dying. They knew what it was from experience and now had no fear for themselves, for the same man was never attacked twice — never at least fatally. Such persons not only received the congratulations of others but, in the elation of the moment, half entertained the vain hope that they were safe from any disease whatsoever in the future.

“How then could we put our trust in such friendship or freedom as we had here? We accepted each other against our inclination. Fear made them court us in war, and us them in peace. Sympathy, the ordinary basis of confidence, was replaced by terror, and fear had more share than friendship in keeping us in the alliance. The first party to be encouraged by the hope of impunity was certain to break faith with the other. So to condemn us for being the first to break off, because they delay the blow that we dread, instead of our delaying to learn for certain whether it will be dealt or not, is to take a false view of the case. For if we were as able as they are to meet their plots and imitate their delay, we should be their equals and under no necessity of being their subjects. But since the liberty of offense is always theirs, the liberty of defense ought clearly to be ours.

In the same summer, after Lesbos had been reduced, the Athenians under Nicias, son of Niceratus, made an expedition against the island of Minoa. It lies off Megara, and the Megarians used it as a fortified post, having built a tower on it. Nicias wanted the Athenians to keep up their blockade from this nearer station instead of from Budorum and Salamis. He meant to stop the Peloponnesian galleys and privateers from slipping out of the island unobserved, as they had been in the habit of doing, and at the same time to keep anything from coming into Megara. So he first took two towers projecting on the side of Nisaea, by engines from the sea, and cleared the entrance to the channel between the island and the shore. He then cut off all communication by building a wall on the mainland, at the point where a bridge over a morass allowed reinforcements to be thrown into the island, which was not far from the continent. A few days were enough to finish this. After that he raised some works on the island itself, left a garrison there, and withdrew with his forces.

“Meanwhile we have plainly shown that it was not for the sake of the Hellenes that you alone then did not Medize, but because the Athenians did not Medize either, and you wished to side with them and be against the rest. Yet you now claim the benefit of good deeds done to please your neighbors. This cannot be admitted. You chose the Athenians, and with them you must stand or fall. Nor can you plead the league then made and claim that it should now protect you. You abandoned that league, and offended against it by helping, instead of hindering, the subjugation of the Aeginetans and other members of it. You did so not under compulsion, but while enjoying the same institutions that you enjoy to the present hour, with no one forcing you as in our case. Lastly, before you were blockaded, an invitation was addressed to you to be neutral and join neither party. This you did not accept. Who then more justly merit the detestation of the Hellenes than you, who sought their ruin under the mask of honor? The former virtues that you allege you now show not to be proper to your character. The real bent of your nature has at length been damningly proved: when the Athenians took the path of injustice, you followed them.

Such were the words of the Thebans. The Lacedaemonian judges decided that the question whether they had received any service from the Plataeans in the war was a fair one for them to put. They had always invited the Plataeans to be neutral, in keeping with the original covenant of Pausanias after the defeat of the Mede, and had again offered them the same conditions definitely before the blockade. The Plataeans had refused this offer, and the judges conceived that, by the loyalty of their own intention, they were now released from the covenant. Having, as they considered, suffered evil at the hands of the Plataeans, they brought them in again one by one and asked each of them the same question, that is, whether they had done the Lacedaemonians and allies any service in the war. When a man said that he had not, they took him out and slew him, without exception. The Plataeans thus massacred numbered not less than two hundred, together with twenty-five Athenians who had shared in the siege. The women were taken as slaves. The Thebans gave the city for about a year to some political emigrants from Megara and to the surviving Plataeans of their own party to inhabit. Afterward they razed it to the ground from the very foundations. Next to the precinct of Hera they built an inn two hundred feet square, with rooms all around above and below, using for this purpose the roofs and doors of the Plataeans. Of the rest of the materials in the wall, the brass and the iron, they made couches, which they dedicated to Hera, and for her they also built a stone chapel a hundred feet square. The land they confiscated and let out on a ten years’ lease to Theban occupiers. The Lacedaemonians’ adverse attitude in the whole Plataean affair was adopted mainly to please the Thebans, who were thought to be useful in the war then raging. Such was the end of Plataea, in the ninety-third year after she became the ally of Athens.

The foundation of this town was evidently meant to annoy Euboea, since the passage across to Cenaeum in that island is a short one. At first it caused some alarm at Athens, which the event, however, did nothing to justify, for the town never gave the Athenians any trouble. The reason was as follows. The Thessalians were sovereign in those parts, and their territory was menaced by the foundation of the town. They were afraid that it might prove a very powerful neighbor, and so they continually harassed and made war on the new settlers, until they wore them out, in spite of their originally considerable numbers, since people flocked from all quarters to a place founded by the Lacedaemonians and therefore thought secure of prosperity. On the other hand, the Lacedaemonians themselves, in the persons of their governors, did their full share toward ruining its prosperity and reducing its population. They frightened away the greater part of the inhabitants by governing harshly and in some cases unfairly, and so made it easier for their neighbors to prevail against them.

At daybreak the two forces united, sat down at the place called Metropolis and encamped. Not long after, the Athenians in the twenty ships entered the Ambracian Gulf to support the Argives, bringing Demosthenes, two hundred Messenian heavy infantry and sixty Athenian archers. While the fleet off Olpae blockaded the hill from the sea, the Acarnanians and a few Amphilochians had already reached Argos. Most of the Amphilochians were held back by force by the Ambraciots. They were making ready to give battle to the enemy, and had chosen Demosthenes to command the whole allied army along with their own generals. Demosthenes led them near Olpae and encamped, a great ravine lying between the two armies. For five days they stayed inactive, and on the sixth both sides drew up in order of battle. The Peloponnesian army was the larger and outflanked its opponents. Demosthenes feared that his right might be surrounded. In a sunken road overgrown with bushes he therefore hid some four hundred heavy infantry and light troops. At the moment of the onset they were to rise behind the enemy’s projecting left wing and attack it in the rear. When both sides were ready, they joined battle. Demosthenes stood on the right wing with the Messenians and a few Athenians. The rest of the line consisted of the different divisions of the Acarnanians and the Amphilochian carters. The Peloponnesians and Ambraciots were drawn up all mixed together, except for the Mantineans, who were massed on the left, though they did not reach the end of the wing. There Eurylochus and his men faced the Messenians and Demosthenes.

The Lacedaemonians saw the Athenians masters of Cythera and expected landings of the same kind on their coasts. They nowhere opposed them in force, but sent garrisons here and there through the country, each made up of as many heavy infantry as the threatened points seemed to require, and for the most part kept strictly on the defensive. They had suffered a severe and unexpected blow on the island, Pylos and Cythera were occupied, and on every side they saw a war whose rapidity defied precaution. They lived in constant fear of internal revolution, and now took the unusual step of raising four hundred horse and a force of archers. They became more timid than ever in military matters, since they found themselves involved in a naval struggle, which their organization had never contemplated, and against Athenians, who always counted an enterprise left unattempted as a success thrown away. Besides this, their numerous recent reverses, coming one upon another without any reason, had thoroughly unnerved them. They were always afraid of a second disaster like that on the island, and so scarcely dared to take the field. They fancied that they could not make a move without a blunder, for they were new to the experience of adversity and had lost all confidence in themselves.

Plans had been settled between the Athenians and their correspondents, both for what was to be said and for what was to be done. The Athenians then sailed by night to Minoa, the island off Megara, with six hundred heavy infantry under Hippocrates, and took post in a quarry not far off, from which bricks used to be dug for the walls. Demosthenes, the other commander, placed himself in ambush with a detachment of Plataean light troops and another of Peripoli, in the precinct of Enyalius, which was still nearer. No one knew of it that night except those whose business it was to know. A little before daybreak the traitors in Megara began to act. For a long time they had been in the habit, every night, of carrying a sculling boat on a cart along the ditch to the sea, and sailing out in it, under pretense of marauding. This gave them a means of opening the gates, and they did it with the consent of the officer in command. They brought the boat back on the cart before day and took it inside the wall through the gates. Their pretended aim was to baffle the Athenian blockade at Minoa, since no boat was to be seen in the harbor. On this occasion the cart was already at the gates, which had been opened in the usual way for the boat. The Athenians, who had agreed on this with the traitors, saw it and ran from the ambush at top speed, to reach the gates before they were shut again and while the cart was still there to keep them from closing. At the same moment their Megarian accomplices killed the guard at the gates. The first to run in was Demosthenes with his Plataeans and Peripoli, at the very spot where the trophy now stands. He was no sooner inside the gates than the Plataeans engaged and defeated the nearest party of Peloponnesians, who had taken the alarm and come to the rescue, and so secured the gates for the Athenian heavy infantry coming up.

Just at this time the Lacedaemonian Brasidas, son of Tellis, happened to be in the neighborhood of Sicyon and Corinth, getting ready an army for Thrace. As soon as he heard that the walls had been taken, he feared for the Peloponnesians in Nisaea and for the safety of Megara. He sent to the Boeotians to meet him as quickly as possible at Tripodiscus, a village of the Megarid so called, under Mount Geraneia. He went there himself with two thousand seven hundred Corinthian heavy infantry, four hundred Phliasians, six hundred Sicyonians, and such troops of his own as he had already levied, expecting to find Nisaea not yet taken. Hearing of its fall (he had marched out by night to Tripodiscus), he took three hundred picked men from the army without waiting until his coming should be known, and came up to Megara unobserved by the Athenians, who were down by the sea. His purpose was, ostensibly, and really if possible, to make an attempt on Nisaea, but above all to get into Megara and secure the town. He accordingly invited the townspeople to admit his party, saying that he had hopes of recovering Nisaea.

Afterwards Brasidas let the allies go home and went back himself to Corinth, to prepare for his expedition to Thrace, his original destination. The Athenians also returned home. The Megarians in the city who were most implicated in the Athenian negotiation knew that they had been detected, and presently disappeared. The rest conferred with the friends of the exiles and restored the party at Pegae, after binding them under solemn oaths to take no vengeance for the past and only to consult the real interests of the town. However, as soon as these men were in office, they held a review of the heavy infantry. They separated the battalions and picked out about a hundred of their enemies, those thought to be most involved in the correspondence with the Athenians. They brought them before the people and compelled the vote to be given openly, and had them condemned and executed, and established a close oligarchy in the town. This revolution lasted a very long while, although effected by a very few partisans.

About the same time in the summer, Brasidas set out on his march to the Thracian places with seventeen hundred heavy infantry. Arriving at Heraclea in Trachis, he sent a messenger from there to his friends at Pharsalus, asking them to conduct him and his army through the country. So there came to Melitia in Achaia Panaerus, Dorus, Hippolochidas, Torylaus and Strophacus, the Chalcidian proxenus, and under their escort he resumed his march. Other Thessalians accompanied him as well, among them Niconidas from Larissa, a friend of Perdiccas. It was never very easy to cross Thessaly without an escort, and throughout Hellas it was a delicate step for an armed force to pass without leave through a neighbor’s country. Besides this, the Thessalian people had always sympathized with the Athenians. Indeed, if Thessaly had had a constitutional government instead of its customary close oligarchy, he would never have been able to go on, since even as it was he was met at the river Enipeus by certain men of the opposite party, who forbade him to go further and complained that he was making the attempt without the consent of the nation. His escort answered that they had no intention of taking him through against their will; they were only friends attending an unexpected visitor. Brasidas himself added that he came as a friend to Thessaly and its inhabitants, that his arms were directed not against them but against the Athenians, with whom he was at war, and that although he knew of no quarrel between the Thessalians and the Lacedaemonians to prevent the two nations from having access to each other’s territory, he neither would nor could go on against their wishes; he could only beg them not to stop him. With this answer they went away. He then took the advice of his escort and pushed on without halting, before a greater force could gather to prevent him. So on the very day he set out from Melitia he covered the whole distance to Pharsalus and encamped on the river Apidanus. From there he went on to Phacium, and from Phacium to Perrhaebia. Here his Thessalian escort turned back, and the Perrhaebians, who are subjects of Thessaly, set him down at Dium in the dominions of Perdiccas. Dium is a Macedonian town under Mount Olympus, facing Thessaly.

“Some of you may hold back because they have private enemies, and fear that I will hand the city over to a party. None need be more at ease than they. I have not come to help this party or that. I would not call it bringing you freedom in any real sense if I ignored your constitution and enslaved the many to the few or the few to the many. That would be heavier than a foreign yoke, and we Lacedaemonians, instead of earning thanks for our trouble, would win neither honor nor glory, but reproaches instead. The very charges that strengthen our hands in the war against the Athenians would, by our own admission, apply to us, and be more hateful in us than in those who make no claim to honesty. For it is more disgraceful for men of character to seize what they covet by plausible fraud than by open force. Force has at least the justification of the might that fortune gives; the other is plain roguery, however clever. A matter that touches us so closely we naturally guard most jealously. And beyond the oaths I have mentioned, what stronger assurance can you have than this: that when you set our words beside the facts, you are convinced it is in our interest to do as we say?

While the Athenians were thus occupied, the Boeotians were mustering at Tanagra. By the time they had come in from all the towns, the Athenians were already on their way home. The rest of the eleven Boeotarchs were against giving battle, because the enemy was no longer in Boeotia; the Athenians had halted just across the Oropian border. But Pagondas, son of Aeolidas, thought it best to risk a battle. He was one of the two Boeotarchs of Thebes (the other being Arianthides, son of Lysimachidas) and was then in supreme command. He called the men to him company by company, so that they would not all leave their arms at once, and urged them to attack the Athenians and face the issue of a battle. He spoke as follows:

Once they had received these instructions for their governments from Xenares, Cleobulus and their friends at Lacedaemon, the Boeotians and Corinthians left. On the road home, two high officials of Argos, who had waited for them there, joined them. These sounded them out on whether the Boeotians might join the Corinthians, Eleans and Mantineans in allying with Argos. Their idea was that, once united, they could make peace or war as they chose, against Lacedaemon or any other power. The Boeotian envoys were pleased to be asked by chance to do the very thing their friends at Lacedaemon had told them to do. The two Argives saw that their proposal was welcome and went away, promising to send ambassadors to the Boeotians. When the Boeotians reached home, they reported to the Boeotarchs what had been said to them at Lacedaemon and by the Argives they had met. The Boeotarchs were pleased with the idea and took it up with all the more eagerness because of the lucky coincidence that Argos was asking for the very thing their friends at Lacedaemon wanted. Soon afterwards ambassadors came from Argos with the proposals described. The Boeotarchs approved the terms and sent the ambassadors away with a promise to send envoys to Argos to negotiate the alliance.

4. No armed force shall be allowed to pass for hostile purposes through the country of the contracting powers, or of the allies in their respective empires, or to go by sea, unless all the cities — that is to say, Athens, Argos, Mantinea and Elis — vote for such passage.

The oath shall be taken at Athens by the Senate and the magistrates, and the Prytanes shall administer it. At Argos, the Senate, the Eighty and the Artynae take it, and the Eighty administer it. At Mantinea, the Demiurgi, the Senate and the other magistrates take it, and the Theori and Polemarchs administer it. At Elis, the Demiurgi, the magistrates and the Six Hundred take it, and the Demiurgi and the Thesmophylaces administer it. The oaths are to be renewed thirty days before the Olympic games, when the Athenians go to Elis, Mantinea and Argos, and ten days before the great feast of the Panathenaea, when the Argives, Mantineans and Eleans go to Athens. The articles of the treaty, the oaths and the alliance are to be inscribed on a stone pillar: by the Athenians in the citadel, by the Argives in the market-place, in the temple of Apollo, and by the Mantineans in the temple of Zeus, in the market-place. The cities are also to erect a brazen pillar jointly at the Olympic games now at hand. If the above cities see good to add anything to these articles, whatever all of them agree upon after consulting together shall be binding.

This proposal was not accepted, so the Eleans tried a second. If the Lacedaemonians objected to restoring Lepreum, they should instead ascend the altar of the Olympian Zeus, since they were so anxious to have access to the temple, and swear before the Hellenes that they would surely pay the fine at a later day. This was also refused, and the Lacedaemonians were excluded from the temple, the sacrifice and the games, and sacrificed at home. The Lepreans were the only other Hellenes who did not attend. Still, the Eleans were afraid that the Lacedaemonians would sacrifice by force, and kept guard with a heavy-armed company of their young men. A thousand Argives and the same number of Mantineans joined them, along with some Athenian cavalry who stayed at Harpina during the feast. Great fears were felt in the assembly that the Lacedaemonians would come in arms, especially after Lichas, son of Arcesilaus, a Lacedaemonian, had been scourged on the course by the umpires. His horses had won, but the Boeotian people were proclaimed the victor, because he had no right to enter. So he came forward on the course and crowned the charioteer, to show that the chariot was his. After this incident all were more afraid than ever and firmly expected a disturbance. The Lacedaemonians, however, kept quiet and let the feast pass by, as we have seen. After the Olympic games, the Argives and the allies went to Corinth to invite her to come over to them. They found some Lacedaemonian envoys there, and a long discussion followed, which ended in nothing, since an earthquake occurred and they dispersed to their different homes.

The next day the Argives and their allies drew up in the order in which they meant to fight if they happened to meet the enemy. The Lacedaemonians were coming back from the water to their old camp by the temple of Heracles. Suddenly they saw their adversaries right in front of them, all in perfect order and advanced from the hill. The Lacedaemonians do not remember ever having experienced a shock like this one. There was hardly any time to prepare. They fell into their ranks at once and in haste, with Agis, their king, directing everything as the law requires. When a king is in the field, every command comes from him. He gives the word to the Polemarchs, they pass it to the Lochages, these to the Pentecostyes, these again to the Enomotarchs, and these last to the Enomoties. All orders needed go the same way and quickly reach the troops. Almost the whole Lacedaemonian army, except for a small part, consists of officers under officers, so the responsibility for what is to be done falls on many.

Melians. But we know that the fortune of war is sometimes more impartial than the disproportion of numbers might lead one to suppose. To submit is to give ourselves over to despair, while action still preserves for us a hope that we may stand erect.

Melians. You may be sure that we are as well aware as you how hard it is to contend against your power and fortune, unless the terms are equal. But we trust that the gods may grant us fortune as good as yours, because we are just men fighting against unjust. And we trust that what we lack in power will be made up by the alliance of the Lacedaemonians, who are bound, if only for very shame, to come to the aid of their kindred. So our confidence, after all, is not so utterly irrational.

“I affirm, then, that in going there you leave many enemies behind you here, and bring more back with you. Perhaps you imagine that the treaty you have made can be trusted. So long as you keep quiet it will go on existing in name (for in name only it has become, through the practices of certain men here and at Sparta). But if you suffered a serious reverse anywhere, our enemies would not hesitate a moment to attack us. The reason is, first, that disaster forced the convention on them and it brought them less honor than it brought us; and second, that the convention itself contains many points still in dispute. Again, some of the most powerful states have never accepted the arrangement at all. Some of them are at open war with us. Others are held back only by truces renewed every ten days, since the Lacedaemonians have not yet moved. And it is only too probable that if they saw our power divided, as we are hurrying to divide it, they would attack us with vigor, together with the Siceliots, whose alliance they would once have valued as they would that of few others. A man ought therefore to weigh these points. He ought not to think of gambling with a country in so critical a position, or of reaching for another empire before we have made the one we hold secure. The Thracian Chalcidians, after all, have been in revolt from us all these years and are still not subdued, and others on the continents obey us only doubtfully. Meanwhile our allies the Egestaeans have been wronged, and we hurry to their help, while the rebels who have wronged us for so long are still waiting for their punishment.

“Be convinced, then, that this adventure abroad will increase our power at home. Let us make the expedition and humble the pride of the Peloponnesians. Let us sail off to Sicily and show them how little we care for the peace we are now enjoying. At the same time we shall either become masters of the whole of Hellas, as we very easily may, through the accession of the Sicilian Hellenes, or at any rate ruin the Syracusans, to the no small advantage of ourselves and our allies. Our navy will secure our freedom to stay if we succeed or to return, for we shall be superior at sea to all the Siceliots put together. Do not let Nicias turn you from your purpose, with the do-nothing policy he advocates and his setting of the young against the old. Follow the good old fashion by which our fathers, old and young together, brought our affairs to their present height by their united counsels, and endeavor still to advance them. Understand that neither youth nor old age can do anything without the other, and that levity, sobriety and deliberate judgment are strongest when united. Understand too that if the city sinks into inaction, it will wear itself out like everything else, and its skill in everything will decay, while each fresh struggle will give it fresh experience and make it more used to defending itself not in word but in deed. In short, my conviction is that a city not inactive by nature could choose no quicker way to ruin itself than by suddenly adopting such a policy. The safest rule of life is to take one’s character and institutions for better and for worse, and to live up to them as closely as one can.”

After this the departure for Sicily took place, at about midsummer. Most of the allies, with the corn transports, the smaller craft and the rest of the expedition, had already been ordered to gather at Corcyra, so as to cross the Ionian Sea from there together to the Iapygian promontory. The Athenians themselves, with those of their allies who happened to be present, went down to Piraeus on the appointed day at daybreak and began to man the ships to put out to sea. The whole population of the city, one may say, went down with them, citizens and foreigners alike. The people of the country each escorted their own, whether friends, relatives or sons, with hope and with lamentation as they went. They thought of the conquests they hoped to make, or of the friends they might never see again, given the long voyage ahead of them, away from their country. At this moment, as they were about to part, the danger came home to them more than when they voted for the expedition. Even so, the strength of the armament and the lavish provision they saw in every department could not but comfort them. The foreigners and the rest of the crowd simply came to see a sight worth seeing and beyond belief.

In Syracuse, meanwhile, reports of the expedition arrived from many quarters, but for a long time nobody believed them at all. An assembly was held, and different orators spoke, as will be seen, some trusting the report of the Athenian expedition and some contradicting it. Among them Hermocrates, son of Hermon, came forward. He was convinced that he knew the truth of the matter, and he gave the following counsel:

“Let us therefore begin our preparations here with confidence. Let us send to some of the Sicels to confirm them, and win the friendship and alliance of others. Let us dispatch envoys to the rest of Sicily to show that the danger is common to all, and to Italy to get its cities to become our allies, or at any rate to refuse to receive the Athenians. I also think it would be best to send to Carthage as well. The Carthaginians are by no means free of apprehension; they live in constant fear that the Athenians may one day attack their city, and they may perhaps think that they themselves would suffer if Sicily were sacrificed. They may be willing to help us secretly if not openly, in one way if not in another. If they will, they are better able to do so than anyone alive today, since they possess the most gold and silver, by which war, like everything else, flourishes. Let us also send to Lacedaemon and Corinth, and ask them to come here and help us as soon as possible, and to keep the war in Hellas alive. But the one thing above all others that I believe we should do at this moment is something that you, with your constitutional love of quiet, will be slow to see, and that I must nevertheless mention. Suppose we Siceliots, all together, or at least as many as possible besides ourselves, were to launch our whole actual navy with two months’ provisions and meet the Athenians at Tarentum and the Iapygian promontory. Suppose we showed them that before fighting for Sicily they must first fight for their passage across the Ionian Sea. We should strike dismay into their army and set them thinking that we have a base for our defensive, since Tarentum is ready to receive us, while they have a wide sea to cross with all their armament. That armament could hardly keep its order through so long a voyage, and since it would come on slowly and in small detachments, it would be easy for us to attack. On the other hand, suppose they lightened their vessels, drew together their fast sailers, and attacked us with these. Then we could fall upon them when they were wearied with rowing, or, if we did not choose to do so, we could retire to Tarentum. They, having crossed with few provisions merely to give battle, would be hard put to it in desolate places. They would have either to remain and be blockaded, or to try to sail along the coast, abandoning the rest of their armament; and they would be further discouraged by not knowing for certain whether the cities would receive them. In my opinion this consideration alone would be enough to deter them from putting out from Corcyra. While they deliberated and reconnoitered our numbers and whereabouts, they would let the season run on until winter was upon them. Or, confounded by so unexpected a circumstance, they would break up the expedition, especially as their most experienced general, as I hear, has taken the command against his will, and would grasp at the first excuse offered by any serious demonstration of ours. We should also be reported, I am certain, as more numerous than we really are. Men’s minds are affected by what they hear; besides, those who are first to attack, or to show that they mean to defend themselves against an attack, inspire greater fear, because men see that they are ready for the emergency. This would be just the case with the Athenians at present. They are attacking us in the belief that we shall not resist, thinking they have a right to judge us severely because we did not help the Lacedaemonians in crushing them. But if they were to see us show a courage for which they are not prepared, they would be more dismayed by the surprise than they could ever be by our actual power. I could wish to persuade you to show this courage. But if that cannot be, at all events lose not a moment in preparing generally for the war. Remember, all of you, that contempt for an assailant is best shown by bravery in action, but that for the present the best course is to accept the preparations that fear inspires as the surest promise of safety, and to act as if the danger were real. That the Athenians are coming to attack us, that they are already on the voyage, and that they are all but here: of this I am sure.”

After this address Nicias at once led the army forward. The Syracusans were not expecting an immediate engagement at that moment, and some had even gone away to the town, which was close by. These now ran up as hard as they could and, though late, took their places here and there in the main body as fast as they joined it. Certainly, neither in this battle nor in the others was the fault of the Syracusans a want of zeal or daring. They were not inferior in courage, so far as their military science could carry them, but when that failed them they were forced to give up their resolution also. On this occasion they had not supposed that the Athenians would begin the attack, and they were forced to stand on their defense at short notice. Even so, they at once took up their arms and advanced to meet them. First the stone-throwers, slingers and archers of both armies began skirmishing, and routed or were routed by one another, as might be expected between light troops. Next, soothsayers brought forward the usual victims, and trumpeters urged on the heavy infantry to the charge. So they advanced. The Syracusans fought for their country, and each individual for his safety that day and his liberty hereafter. In the enemy’s army, the Athenians fought to make another’s country theirs and to save their own from suffering by their defeat. The Argives and the independent allies fought to help them get what they had come for, and to earn by victory another sight of the country they had left behind. The subject allies owed most of their ardor to the desire for self-preservation, which they could hope for only if victorious. Next to this, as a secondary motive, came the chance of serving on easier terms after helping the Athenians to a fresh conquest.

The Syracusans heard him out and voted everything as he advised. They elected three generals: Hermocrates himself, Heraclides, son of Lysimachus, and Sicanus, son of Execestes. They also sent envoys to Corinth and Lacedaemon to obtain a force of allies to join them. The envoys were to persuade the Lacedaemonians to take up the war against the Athenians openly and in real earnest, for the Syracusans’ sake, so that the Athenians might either have to leave Sicily or be less able to send reinforcements to their army there.

Meanwhile the Syracusan envoys sent to Corinth and Lacedaemon were working their way along the coast, trying to persuade the Italiots to oppose the Athenians, whose proceedings threatened Italy as much as Syracuse. At Corinth the envoys made a speech asking for help on the ground of their common origin. The Corinthians voted at once to give it themselves, wholeheartedly, and then sent envoys along with them to Lacedaemon to help persuade her too to wage the war on the Athenians more openly at home, and to send succors to Sicily. When the Corinthian envoys reached Lacedaemon, they found Alcibiades there with his fellow refugees. He had crossed at once from Thurii in a trading vessel, first to Cyllene in Elis and then on to Lacedaemon, upon the Lacedaemonians’ own invitation and with a safe conduct obtained first, since he feared them because of his part in the affair of Mantinea. So in the assembly of the Lacedaemonians the Corinthians, the Syracusans and Alcibiades all pressed the same request, and persuaded them. But the ephors and the authorities resolved only to send envoys to Syracuse to stop it from surrendering to the Athenians. They showed no inclination to send any help. Alcibiades then came forward and stirred up and inflamed the Lacedaemonians with the following speech:

“I must first speak to you about the prejudice against me, so that suspicion may not make you unwilling to hear me on public affairs. The connection with you as your proxeni had been renounced by my family’s ancestors out of some discontent. I personally tried to renew it by my good offices toward you, in particular at the time of the disaster at Pylos. Yet although I kept up this friendly attitude, you chose to make the peace with the Athenians through my enemies, and so to strengthen them and discredit me. You had no right, then, to complain when I turned to the Mantineans and Argives and took other opportunities to thwart and injure you. The time has now come for those of you who may have been unfairly angry with me in the bitterness of that moment to see the matter in its true light and take a different view. Others judged me unfavorably because I leaned toward the commons. They should not think their dislike any better founded. We have always been enemies of tyrants, and everyone who opposes arbitrary power is called commons. For that reason we continued as leaders of the multitude. Besides, democracy being the government of the city, in most things we had to conform to existing conditions. Still, we tried to be more moderate than the licentious temper of the times. Others, then as now, tried to lead the multitude astray — the very men who banished me. Our party was that of the whole people. Our creed was to do our part in preserving the form of government under which the city had enjoyed the utmost greatness and freedom, and which we had found in place. As for democracy, the men of sense among us knew what it was, and I perhaps as well as any, since I have more reason to complain of it. But there is nothing new to be said about a patent absurdity. And we did not think it safe to change it while you were pressing us with your hostility.

“Meanwhile I hope that none of you will think the worse of me because I, who until now passed for a lover of my country, am now actively joining its worst enemies to attack it. I hope too that you will not distrust my words as the product of an outlaw’s zeal. I am an outlaw through the iniquity of those who drove me out, but not, if you will be guided by me, from serving you. My worst enemies are not you, who only harmed your foes, but those who forced their friends to turn into enemies. When I am wronged I do not feel love of country. I felt it when I was secure in my rights as a citizen. In fact I do not think I am now attacking a country that is still mine. I am trying instead to win back one that is mine no longer. The true lover of his country is not the one who submits to losing it unjustly instead of attacking it. He is the one whose longing for it is so great that he will stop at nothing to recover it. For myself, Lacedaemonians, I beg you therefore to employ me without scruple in danger and hardship of every kind. Bear in mind the saying that everyone repeats: if I did you great harm as an enemy, I can also do you good service as a friend, since I know the plans of the Athenians and only guessed at yours. And I entreat you to believe, for your own part, that your most vital interests are now being weighed. Send the expeditions to Sicily and Attica without hesitation. With only a small part of your forces present, you will save important cities in that island and destroy the power of Athens, as it is now and as it may become. After that you will live in security and hold the supremacy over all Hellas, resting not on force but on consent and affection.”

Such were the contents of Nicias’s letter. When the Athenians had heard it, they refused to accept his resignation. Instead they chose him two colleagues, naming Menander and Euthydemus, two of the officers at the seat of war, to fill their places until the others arrived, so that Nicias would not be left alone in his sickness to bear the whole weight of affairs. They also voted to send out another army and navy, drawn partly from the Athenians on the muster-roll and partly from the allies. The colleagues chosen for Nicias were Demosthenes, son of Alcisthenes, and Eurymedon, son of Thucles. Eurymedon was sent off at once, about the time of the winter solstice, with ten ships and a hundred and twenty talents of silver, and with instructions to tell the army that reinforcements would arrive and that care would be taken of them. Demosthenes stayed behind to organize the expedition. He meant to start as soon as it was spring, sent to the allies for troops, and meanwhile got together money, ships and heavy infantry at home.

After the Sicel disaster the Syracusans put off any immediate attack on the Athenians. Demosthenes and Eurymedon, whose forces from Corcyra and the mainland were now ready, crossed the Ionian Gulf with their whole armament to the Iapygian promontory. From there they started and touched at the Choerades Isles, off Iapygia, where they took on board a hundred and fifty Iapygian darters of the Messapian tribe. They renewed an old friendship with Artas the chief, who had supplied them with the darters, and arrived at Metapontium in Italy. Here they persuaded their allies the Metapontines to send three hundred darters and two galleys with them, and with this reinforcement they coasted on to Thurii. There they found that the party hostile to Athens had recently been expelled by a revolution, and so they stayed to muster and review the whole army, to see if any had been left behind, and to prevail on the Thurians to join their expedition wholeheartedly and, in the circumstances in which they found themselves, to conclude a defensive and offensive alliance with the Athenians.

The engagement of the rest was more voluntary. What persuaded the Dorian Argives to join the Ionian Athenians in a war against Dorians was less the league than hatred of the Lacedaemonians and the immediate private advantage of each individual. The Mantineans and other Arcadian mercenaries were accustomed to go against whatever enemy was pointed out to them at the moment, and interest led them to regard the Arcadians serving with the Corinthians as just as much their enemies as anyone else. The Cretans and Aetolians also served for hire. The Cretans had joined the Rhodians in founding Gela, and they thus came to consent to fight for pay against their colonists instead of for them. There were also some Acarnanians serving for pay, although they came chiefly out of love for Demosthenes and goodwill to the Athenians, whose allies they were. All these lived on the Hellenic side of the Ionian Gulf. Of the Italiots, there were the Thurians and Metapontines, dragged into the quarrel by the stern necessities of a time of revolution. Of the Siceliots, there were the Naxians and the Catanians. Of the barbarians, there were the Egestaeans, who had called in the Athenians, most of the Sicels, and, from outside Sicily, some Tyrrhenian enemies of Syracuse and Iapygian mercenaries.
