“With us it is different. The original estimate of ourselves, which gave us courage in the days of our unskillfulness, has been strengthened. To it has been added the conviction that we must be the best seamen of the time, if we have conquered the best. This has given every man among us a double measure of hope, and for the most part, where there is the greatest hope, there is also the greatest ardor for action. The means they have tried to find to combat us, by copying our armament, are familiar to our way of fighting and will be met with proper provisions. They will never be able to carry a number of heavy infantry on their decks, contrary to their custom, and a number of darters (born landsmen, one may say, Acarnanians and others, put afloat, who will not know how to discharge their weapons when they have to keep still), without hampering their ships and falling into confusion among themselves, through fighting not according to their own tactics. For they will gain nothing by the number of their ships. I say this to those of you who may be alarmed at having to fight against odds. A quantity of ships in a confined space will only be slower in executing the movements required, and most exposed to injury from our means of offense. Indeed, if you would know the plain truth, as we are credibly informed, the excess of their sufferings and the necessities of their present distress have made them desperate. They have no confidence in their force, but wish to try their fortune in the only way they can, either to force their passage and sail out, or after this to retreat by land, since it is impossible for them to be worse off than they are.

Meanwhile the two armies on shore, while victory hung in the balance, were a prey to the most agonizing and conflicting emotions. The natives thirsted for more glory than they had already won, while the invaders feared to find themselves in even worse plight than before. Because everything the Athenians had was staked on their fleet, their fear for the outcome was like nothing they had ever felt, and their view of the struggle was necessarily as varied as the battle itself. They were close to the action and were not all looking at the same point at once. Some saw their friends winning, took courage, and called on heaven not to deprive them of safety. Others had their eyes on the losers; they wailed and cried aloud, and though only spectators, they were more overcome than the actual combatants. Others again were gazing at some spot where the battle was evenly disputed. As the struggle dragged on without decision, their swaying bodies reflected the agitation of their minds, and they suffered the worst agony of all, ever just within reach of safety or just on the point of destruction. In short, in that one Athenian army, as long as the sea-fight remained doubtful, every sound was to be heard at once: shrieks, cheers, “We win,” “We lose,” and all the other cries that a great host would necessarily utter in great peril. It was nearly the same with the men in the fleet. At last, after the battle had lasted a long while, the Syracusans and their allies put the Athenians to flight and chased them in open rout to the shore, with much shouting and cheering. The naval force, some one way and some another, ran ashore, all those not taken afloat, and rushed from their ships to the camp. The army was no longer divided but carried away by one impulse, and all deplored what had happened with shrieks and groans. Some ran down to help the ships, others to guard what was left of their wall, while the remaining and most numerous part already began to consider how they should save themselves. Indeed, the panic of that moment had never been surpassed. They now suffered very nearly what they had inflicted at Pylos. Then the Lacedaemonians, with the loss of their fleet, had also lost the men who had crossed over to the island; so now the Athenians had no hope of escaping by land, without the help of some extraordinary accident.

The emissaries of Pharnabazus and Tissaphernes negotiated separately, and a keen competition now arose at Lacedaemon over whether a fleet and army should be sent first to Ionia and Chios, or to the Hellespont. The Lacedaemonians, however, decidedly favored the Chians and Tissaphernes, who were backed by Alcibiades, the family friend of Endius, one of the ephors for that year. Indeed, this is how their house got its Laconic name: Alcibiades was the family name of Endius. Nevertheless the Lacedaemonians first sent Phrynis, one of the Perioeci, to Chios, to see whether the Chians had as many ships as they said and whether their city was generally as great as reported. When he brought word that they had been told the truth, the Lacedaemonians immediately made an alliance with the Chians and Erythraeans and voted to send them forty ships. According to the Chians, there were already not less than sixty in the island. At first the Lacedaemonians meant to send ten of these forty themselves, with Melanchridas as their admiral. But afterwards an earthquake occurred, and they sent Chalcideus instead of Melanchridas, and equipped only five ships in Laconia instead of ten. And the winter ended, and with it ended the nineteenth year of this war of which Thucydides is the historian.

While the Chians were busy with this, toward the end of the same summer a force sailed from Athens in forty-eight ships, some of them transports. It consisted of a thousand Athenian heavy infantry, fifteen hundred Argives (five hundred of them light troops equipped with armor by the Athenians) and a thousand men from the allies. Phrynichus, Onomacles and Scironides commanded it. It put in at Samos, crossed over, and encamped at Miletus. The Milesians then came out against the Athenians and their allies, with eight hundred heavy infantry, the Peloponnesians who had arrived with Chalcideus, some foreign mercenaries of Tissaphernes, and Tissaphernes himself with his cavalry. The Argives, on their own wing, charged forward with the careless disdain of men advancing against Ionians who would never withstand their attack, and the Milesians defeated them, killing little short of three hundred. The Athenians, for their part, first defeated the Peloponnesians and drove the barbarians and the rabble of the army before them. They did not engage the Milesians, who had seen the Argives routed and retreated into the town. The Athenians then crowned their victory by grounding their arms right under the walls of Miletus. So in this battle the Ionians on both sides overcame the Dorians: the Athenians beat the Peloponnesians opposed to them, and the Milesians beat the Argives. After setting up a trophy, the Athenians prepared to build a wall around the town, which stood on an isthmus. They thought that if they gained Miletus, the other towns would easily come over to them.

The same winter the Athenians at Samos were joined by thirty-five more vessels from home under Charminus, Strombichides and Euctemon. They called in their squadron at Chios and all the rest, intending to blockade Miletus with their navy and to send a fleet and an army against Chios, and they drew lots for the respective services. They carried out this plan. Strombichides, Onamacles and Euctemon, to whom Chios fell by lot, sailed against it with thirty ships and a part of the thousand heavy infantry who had been at Miletus, carried in transports. The rest stayed at Samos with seventy-four ships, held command of the sea, and advanced on Miletus.

Meanwhile the Athenian armament, sailing around Corycus, fell in with three Chian warships off Arginus and gave immediate chase. A great storm came on, and the Chians took refuge in the harbor with difficulty. The three Athenian vessels that were furthest forward in the pursuit were wrecked and thrown up near the city of Chios, and their crews were killed or taken prisoner. The rest of the Athenian fleet took refuge in the harbor called Phoenicus, under Mount Mimas, and afterwards put into Lesbos from there and prepared for the work of fortification.

Alcibiades also advised Tissaphernes not to be in too great a hurry to end the war. He should refuse to be persuaded to bring up the Phoenician fleet that he was equipping, or to provide pay for more Hellenes, and so put the power by land and sea into the same hands. He should leave each of the contending parties in possession of one element, so that the king could call in the other whenever he found one troublesome. For if the command of the sea and land were united in one hand, the king would not know where to turn for help to overthrow the dominant power, unless he finally chose to stand up himself and go through with the struggle at great expense and hazard. The cheapest plan was to let the Hellenes wear each other out, at a small share of the expense and without risk to himself. Besides, he would find the Athenians the most convenient partners in empire, since they did not aim at conquests on land, and carried on the war on principles and in a manner most advantageous to the King. They were prepared to combine to conquer the sea for Athens, and for the King all the Hellenes inhabiting his country, whom the Peloponnesians, on the contrary, had come to liberate. Now it was not likely that the Lacedaemonians would free the Hellenes from the Hellenic Athenians without also freeing them from the barbarian Mede, unless he overthrew them first. Alcibiades therefore urged him to wear both sides out at first, and, after cutting down the Athenian power as far as he could, to rid the country of the Peloponnesians without delay. In the main Tissaphernes approved of this policy, so far at least as could be judged from his behavior. He now gave his confidence to Alcibiades in return for his good advice, and kept the Peloponnesians short of money. He would not let them fight at sea, and ruined their cause by pretending that the Phoenician fleet would arrive and that they would then be able to fight with the odds in their favor. In this way he made their navy, which had been very remarkable, lose its efficiency, and he showed a coolness toward the war that was too plain to be mistaken.

Alcibiades gave this advice to Tissaphernes and the King, with whom he then was. He did so not merely because he thought it really the best, but because he was looking for means to bring about his restoration to his country. He knew well that if he did not destroy it, he might one day hope to persuade the Athenians to recall him, and he thought his best chance of persuading them lay in letting them see that he had the favor of Tissaphernes. The event proved him right. The Athenians at Samos learned that he had influence with Tissaphernes. They found this out mainly on their own initiative (though partly also through Alcibiades himself, who sent word to their chief men to tell the best men in the army that he would be glad to return to his country and make Tissaphernes their friend, if only there were an oligarchy in place of the rascally democracy that had banished him). Upon this the captains and chief men in the armament at once embraced the idea of subverting the democracy.

After this the Chians were besieged even more closely than before by land and sea, and the famine in the place was great. Meanwhile the Athenian envoys with Pisander arrived at the court of Tissaphernes and conferred with him about the proposed agreement. But Alcibiades was not altogether sure of Tissaphernes (who feared the Peloponnesians more than the Athenians and besides wished to wear out both parties, as Alcibiades himself had recommended). So he resorted to the following stratagem to make the treaty between the Athenians and Tissaphernes fail through the magnitude of his demands. In my opinion Tissaphernes wanted this result, his motive being fear. Alcibiades, for his part, now saw that Tissaphernes was determined not to treat on any terms, and he wished the Athenians to think, not that he was unable to persuade Tissaphernes, but that Tissaphernes had been persuaded and was willing to join them, and that they had not conceded enough to him. For the demands of Alcibiades, who spoke for Tissaphernes while he was present, were so extravagant that the Athenians had to bear the blame of the failure, although for a long while they agreed to whatever he asked. He required the cession of the whole of Ionia, then of the adjacent islands, besides other concessions, and these passed without opposition. At last, in the third interview, Alcibiades, who now feared that his inability would be completely discovered, required them to allow the King to build ships and sail along his own coast wherever he pleased and with as many ships as he pleased. At this the Athenians would yield no further. They concluded that nothing could be done and that they had been deceived by Alcibiades, and they went away in a passion and proceeded to Samos.

After encouraging each other in these resolutions, they at once sent off half the envoys together with Pisander to do what was necessary at Athens (with instructions to establish oligarchies on their way in all the subject cities they might touch at). The other half they dispatched in different directions to the other dependencies. Diitrephes also, who was in the neighborhood of Chios and had been elected to the command of the Thracian towns, was sent off to his government. Arriving at Thasos, he abolished the democracy there. Two months, however, had not passed after his departure before the Thasians began to fortify their town. They were already tired of an aristocracy under Athens and were expecting freedom from Lacedaemon every day. Indeed there was a party of them (whom the Athenians had banished) who were with the Peloponnesians. With their friends in the town they were already making every effort to bring a squadron and effect the revolt of Thasos. So this party saw exactly what it most wanted done, namely the reform of the government without risk and the abolition of the democracy that would have opposed it. Things at Thasos thus turned out just the opposite of what the oligarchical conspirators at Athens expected. The same, in my opinion, was the case in many of the other dependencies. The cities no sooner got a moderate government and liberty of action than they went on to absolute freedom, and were not at all seduced by the show of reform offered by the Athenians.

But this was a mere catchword for the multitude, since the authors of the revolution were in fact to govern. Still, the Assembly and the Council of the Bean went on meeting. They discussed nothing that the conspirators had not approved, and the conspirators supplied the speakers and reviewed in advance what they would say. Fear, and the sight of how many the conspirators were, shut the mouths of everyone else. If anyone did venture to speak against them, he was soon put to death in some convenient way. No one searched for the murderers, and no justice could be had against them even if they were suspected. The people stayed motionless, so thoroughly cowed that men counted themselves lucky to escape violence even when they kept silent. An exaggerated belief in the number of the conspirators also demoralized the people. The size of the city left them helpless, they had no understanding with one another, and they had no means of finding out how many the conspirators really were. For the same reason no one could open his grief to a neighbor and concert measures to defend himself, since he would have had to speak either to a man he did not know, or to a man he knew but did not trust. Indeed the whole popular party approached one another with suspicion, each thinking his neighbor a party to what was going on. The conspirators had in their ranks men whom no one could ever have believed capable of joining an oligarchy, and it was these men who made the many so suspicious. By confirming the commons in their mistrust of one another, they helped to secure impunity for the few.

Agis, however, did not believe the city was tranquil, or that the commons would surrender their ancient liberty in a moment. He thought that the sight of a large Lacedaemonian force would excite them, if they were not already in commotion, of which he was by no means certain. So he gave the envoys of the Four Hundred an answer that offered no hope of an accommodation. He sent for large reinforcements from Peloponnese, and not long afterwards came down to the very walls of Athens with these troops and his garrison from Decelea. He hoped that civil disturbances might help to bring the Athenians to his terms, or that in the confusion to be expected inside and outside the city they might even surrender without a blow. At all events he thought he would succeed in seizing the Long Walls, stripped of their defenders. However, the Athenians watched him come close up without causing the least disturbance within the city. They sent out their cavalry and a number of heavy infantry, light troops, and archers, who shot down some of his soldiers that came too near and took some arms and dead. At last Agis was convinced. He led his army back, stayed with his own troops in their old position at Decelea, and after a few days in Attica sent the reinforcement home. After this the Four Hundred persisted and sent another embassy to Agis, and now they got a better reception. At his suggestion they dispatched envoys to Lacedaemon to negotiate a treaty, being desirous of making peace.

Meanwhile the chiefs at Samos, and especially Thrasybulus, had remained firmly resolved to recall Alcibiades from the moment he changed the government. At last, in an assembly, they won over the mass of the soldiers. The soldiers voted for the recall and amnesty of Alcibiades, and the chiefs sailed over to Tissaphernes and brought Alcibiades to Samos. They were convinced that their only chance of safety lay in Alcibiades drawing Tissaphernes away from the Peloponnesians and over to themselves. An assembly was then held. In it Alcibiades complained of his private misfortune in having been banished and lamented it. He spoke at great length on public affairs, raised their hopes for the future very high, and extravagantly magnified his own influence with Tissaphernes. His aims were to frighten the oligarchical government at Athens, to hasten the dissolution of the clubs, to increase his credit with the army at Samos and strengthen their own confidence, and finally to turn the enemy as strongly as possible against Tissaphernes and destroy the hopes they had placed in him. So Alcibiades held out to the army promises as extravagant as these: Tissaphernes had solemnly assured him that if he could only trust the Athenians, they would never go short of supplies while he had anything left, no, not even if he had to coin his own silver couch; and he would bring the Phoenician fleet, now at Aspendus, to the Athenians instead of to the Peloponnesians. But he could trust the Athenians only if Alcibiades were recalled to be his security for them.
